claim: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) is an indispensable cofactor in all domains of life.
source: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) is an indispensable cofactor in all domains of life, and its homeostasis must be regulated tightly.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in biochemistry supported by the cited literature (Belenky et al., 2007; Magni et al., 2004) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: MsNrtR (MSMEG_3198) controls the de novo pathway of NAD+ biosynthesis in M. smegmatis.
source: Here we report that a Nudix-related transcriptional factor, designated MsNrtR (MSMEG_3198), controls the de novo pathway of NAD+biosynthesis in M. smegmatis, a non-tuberculosis Mycobacterium.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data presented in the manuscript including RT-qPCR, NAD+ measurements, and genetic assays shown in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: MsNrtR is an auto-repressor that negatively controls the de novo NAD+ biosynthetic pathway.
source: The integrated evidence in vitro and in vivo confirms that MsNrtR is an auto-repressor, which negatively controls the de novo NAD+biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including lacZ fusion assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and RT-qPCR analyses (Figure 4B) showing increased expression upon nrtR deletion.

claim: Binding of MsNrtR to cognate DNA can be disrupted by an ADP-ribose intermediate.
source: Binding of MsNrtR cognate DNA is finely mapped, and can be disrupted by an ADP-ribose intermediate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 demonstrating that 50 mM of ADP-ribose can significantly release MsNrtR from DNA.

claim: The acetylation of MsNrtR at Lysine 134 participates in the homeostasis of intracellular NAD+ level in M. smegmatis.
source: Unexpectedly, we discover that the acetylation of MsNrtR at Lysine 134 participates in the homeostasis of intra-cellular NAD+ level in M. smegmatis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that K134 point mutations lead to altered NAD+ and NADH levels (Figure 7C-D) and changes in transcriptional regulation (Figure 7A-B).

claim: NrtR acetylation proceeds via the non-enzymatic acetyl-phosphate (AcP) route rather than by the enzymatic Pat/CobB pathway.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that NrtR acetylation proceeds via the non-enzymatic acetyl-phosphate (AcP) route rather than by the enzymatic Pat/CobB pathway.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro acetylation assays with AcP (Figure 6D-G) and in vivo genetic experiments with ackA and pta mutants (Figure 6H-I), as well as the lack of effect from pat/cobB deletions (Figure 6C).

claim: Acetylation occurs on the paralogs of NrtR in the Gram-positive bacterium Streptococcus and the Gram-negative bacterium Vibrio.
source: In addition, the acetylation also occurs on the paralogs of NrtR in the Gram-positive bacterium Streptococcus and the Gram-negative bacterium Vibrio, suggesting that these proteins have a common mechanism of post-translational modification in the context of NAD+ homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 detecting acetylation in NrtR homologs from Vibrio cholerae and Streptococcus suis.

claim: NAD+ acts as an electron carrier in redox reactions.
source: It not only acts as an electron carrier in redox reactions (Belenky et al., 2007; Magni et al., 2004), but also functions as a co-substrate for a number of non-redox enzymes (DNA ligase [Wilkinson et al., 2001], NAD+-dependent de-acetylase CobB/Sir-2 [Schmidt et al., 2004] and ADP-ribose transferase [Domenighini and Rappuoli, 1996]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature (Belenky et al., 2007; Magni et al., 2004) and represents established biochemical knowledge.

claim: NAD+ functions as a co-substrate for DNA ligase.
source: It not only acts as an electron carrier in redox reactions (Belenky et al., 2007; Magni et al., 2004), but also functions as a co-substrate for a number of non-redox enzymes (DNA ligase [Wilkinson et al., 2001], NAD+-dependent de-acetylase CobB/Sir-2 [Schmidt et al., 2004] and ADP-ribose transferase [Domenighini and Rappuoli, 1996]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilkinson et al., 2001.

claim: NAD+ functions as a co-substrate for NAD+-dependent de-acetylase CobB/Sir-2.
source: It not only acts as an electron carrier in redox reactions (Belenky et al., 2007; Magni et al., 2004), but also functions as a co-substrate for a number of non-redox enzymes (DNA ligase [Wilkinson et al., 2001], NAD+-dependent de-acetylase CobB/Sir-2 [Schmidt et al., 2004] and ADP-ribose transferase [Domenighini and Rappuoli, 1996]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2004.

claim: NAD+ functions as a co-substrate for ADP-ribose transferase.
source: It not only acts as an electron carrier in redox reactions (Belenky et al., 2007; Magni et al., 2004), but also functions as a co-substrate for a number of non-redox enzymes (DNA ligase [Wilkinson et al., 2001], NAD+-dependent de-acetylase CobB/Sir-2 [Schmidt et al., 2004] and ADP-ribose transferase [Domenighini and Rappuoli, 1996]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Domenighini and Rappuoli, 1996.

claim: The intracellular level of NAD+ is dependent on the de novo synthesis pathway and/or its salvage or recycling route.
source: The intra-cellular level of NAD+ is dependent on the de novo synthesis pathway and/or its salvage or recycling route (Gazzaniga et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gazzaniga et al., 2009 and represents established knowledge in NAD+ metabolism.

claim: NAD+ synthesis in eukaryotes begins with tryptophan as a primer.
source: Unlike NAD+ synthesis in eukaryotes, which begins with tryptophan as a primer (Kurnasov et al., 2003), NAD+ in most prokaryotes is produced de novo from the amino acid aspartate (Kurnasov et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kurnasov et al., 2003.

claim: NAD+ in most prokaryotes is produced de novo from the amino acid aspartate.
source: Unlike NAD+ synthesis in eukaryotes, which begins with tryptophan as a primer (Kurnasov et al., 2003), NAD+ in most prokaryotes is produced de novo from the amino acid aspartate (Kurnasov et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kurnasov et al., 2003.

claim: Certain bacterial species have evolved salvage pathways to produce NAD+ by recycling nicotinic acid.
source: Also, certain species have evolved salvage pathway to produce NAD+ (Figure 1) by recycling its precursor metabolites ranging from nicotinic acid (Na) (Boshoff et al., 2008) to nicotinamide (Nam) (Boshoff et al., 2008) and nicotinamide riboside (RNam) (Rodionov et al., 2008a; Kurnasov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boshoff et al., 2008 and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Certain bacterial species have evolved salvage pathways to produce NAD+ by recycling nicotinamide.
source: Also, certain species have evolved salvage pathway to produce NAD+ (Figure 1) by recycling its precursor metabolites ranging from nicotinic acid (Na) (Boshoff et al., 2008) to nicotinamide (Nam) (Boshoff et al., 2008) and nicotinamide riboside (RNam) (Rodionov et al., 2008a; Kurnasov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boshoff et al., 2008 and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Certain bacterial species have evolved salvage pathways to produce NAD+ by recycling nicotinamide riboside.
source: Also, certain species have evolved salvage pathway to produce NAD+ (Figure 1) by recycling its precursor metabolites ranging from nicotinic acid (Na) (Boshoff et al., 2008) to nicotinamide (Nam) (Boshoff et al., 2008) and nicotinamide riboside (RNam) (Rodionov et al., 2008a; Kurnasov et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rodionov et al., 2008a; Kurnasov et al., 2002 and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Tight regulation of NAD+ homeostasis is needed to prevent the accumulation of harmful intermediates.
source: Tight regulation of NAD+ homeostasis is needed to prevent the accumulation of harmful intermediates (Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2009.

claim: Three types of regulatory systems have been described for NAD+ biosynthesis and/or salvage.
source: In fact, three types of regulatory systems have been described for NAD+ biosynthesis and/or salvage.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent discussion of NadR, NiaR, and NrtR regulators with citations to relevant literature.

claim: NadR and NiaR are well-known regulatory proteins for NAD+ metabolism.
source: In addition to the two well-known regulatory proteins (NadR [Gerasimova and Gelfand, 2005; Raffaelli et al., 1999] and NiaR [Rodionov et al., 2008a]), a family of Nudix-related transcriptional regulators (NrtR) was initially proposed via bioinformatics (Rodionov et al., 2008b) and recently validated in Streptococcus suis (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerasimova and Gelfand, 2005; Raffaelli et al., 1999 for NadR and Rodionov et al., 2008a for NiaR.

claim: NrtR was initially proposed via bioinformatics.
source: In addition to the two well-known regulatory proteins (NadR [Gerasimova and Gelfand, 2005; Raffaelli et al., 1999] and NiaR [Rodionov et al., 2008a]), a family of Nudix-related transcriptional regulators (NrtR) was initially proposed via bioinformatics (Rodionov et al., 2008b) and recently validated in Streptococcus suis (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodionov et al., 2008b.

claim: NrtR was recently validated in Streptococcus suis.
source: In addition to the two well-known regulatory proteins (NadR [Gerasimova and Gelfand, 2005; Raffaelli et al., 1999] and NiaR [Rodionov et al., 2008a]), a family of Nudix-related transcriptional regulators (NrtR) was initially proposed via bioinformatics (Rodionov et al., 2008b) and recently validated in Streptococcus suis (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: The paradigm NadR protein of Enterobacteriaceae has three different functional domains.
source: The paradigm NadR protein of Enterobacteriaceae is unusual in that it has three different functional domains (Grose et al., 2005): i) the N-terminal transcriptional repressor domain (Grose et al., 2005; Penfound and Foster, 1999); the central domain of a weak adenylyltransferase (Raffaelli et al., 1999; Grose et al., 2005), and the C-terminal domain of nicotinamide ribose kinase (Kurnasov et al., 2002; Grose et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Grose et al., 2005; Penfound and Foster, 1999; Raffaelli et al., 1999; Kurnasov et al., 2002).

claim: NadR has an N-terminal transcriptional repressor domain.
source: The paradigm NadR protein of Enterobacteriaceae is unusual in that it has three different functional domains (Grose et al., 2005): i) the N-terminal transcriptional repressor domain (Grose et al., 2005; Penfound and Foster, 1999); the central domain of a weak adenylyltransferase (Raffaelli et al., 1999; Grose et al., 2005), and the C-terminal domain of nicotinamide ribose kinase (Kurnasov et al., 2002; Grose et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grose et al., 2005; Penfound and Foster, 1999.

claim: NadR has a central domain with weak adenylyltransferase activity.
source: The paradigm NadR protein of Enterobacteriaceae is unusual in that it has three different functional domains (Grose et al., 2005): i) the N-terminal transcriptional repressor domain (Grose et al., 2005; Penfound and Foster, 1999); the central domain of a weak adenylyltransferase (Raffaelli et al., 1999; Grose et al., 2005), and the C-terminal domain of nicotinamide ribose kinase (Kurnasov et al., 2002; Grose et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raffaelli et al., 1999; Grose et al., 2005.

claim: NadR has a C-terminal domain with nicotinamide ribose kinase activity.
source: The paradigm NadR protein of Enterobacteriaceae is unusual in that it has three different functional domains (Grose et al., 2005): i) the N-terminal transcriptional repressor domain (Grose et al., 2005; Penfound and Foster, 1999); the central domain of a weak adenylyltransferase (Raffaelli et al., 1999; Grose et al., 2005), and the C-terminal domain of nicotinamide ribose kinase (Kurnasov et al., 2002; Grose et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kurnasov et al., 2002; Grose et al., 2005.

claim: NadR is a NAD+ liganded regulator.
source: NadR is a NAD+ liganded regulator (Penfound and Foster, 1999), whereas NiaR is a nicotinic acid-responsive repressor in most species of Bacillus and Clostridium (Rodionov et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Penfound and Foster, 1999.

claim: NiaR is a nicotinic acid-responsive repressor in most species of Bacillus and Clostridium.
source: NadR is a NAD+ liganded regulator (Penfound and Foster, 1999), whereas NiaR is a nicotinic acid-responsive repressor in most species of Bacillus and Clostridium (Rodionov et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodionov et al., 2008a.

claim: The prototypic NrtR possesses dual functions: Nudix-like hydrolase and DNA-binding/repressor.
source: Although the prototypic NrtR possesses dual functions (Nudix-like hydrolase and DNA-binding/repressor) (Huang et al., 2009; Rodionov et al., 2008b), the NrtR homolog in S. suis seems to be an evolutionarily remnant regulator that lacks enzymatic activity (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2009; Rodionov et al., 2008b.

claim: The NrtR homolog in S. suis lacks enzymatic activity.
source: Although the prototypic NrtR possesses dual functions (Nudix-like hydrolase and DNA-binding/repressor) (Huang et al., 2009; Rodionov et al., 2008b), the NrtR homolog in S. suis seems to be an evolutionarily remnant regulator that lacks enzymatic activity (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: NrtR is widely distributed across diversified species.
source: The phylogeny of NrtR suggests that it is widely distributed across diversified species (Huang et al., 2009; Rodionov et al., 2008b; Wang et al., 2019), and that its regulation of central NAD+ metabolism contributes to the virulence of an opportunistic pathogen, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Okon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2009; Rodionov et al., 2008b; Wang et al., 2019 and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: NrtR regulation of central NAD+ metabolism contributes to the virulence of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: The phylogeny of NrtR suggests that it is widely distributed across diversified species (Huang et al., 2009; Rodionov et al., 2008b; Wang et al., 2019), and that its regulation of central NAD+ metabolism contributes to the virulence of an opportunistic pathogen, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Okon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Okon et al., 2017.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis exploits flexible metabolism to establish persistent infection within the host.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a successful pathogen in that it exploits flexible metabolism to establish persistent infection within the host, resulting in the disease of tuberculosis (TB) (Bi et al., 2011; Shiloh and Champion, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bi et al., 2011; Shiloh and Champion, 2010.

claim: The de novo synthesis of NAD+ balances NAD+ metabolism together with an alternative salvage route.
source: Together with an alternative salvage route, the de novo synthesis of NAD+ balances NAD+ metabolism (Boshoff et al., 2008; Bi et al., 2011) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boshoff et al., 2008; Bi et al., 2011 and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The removal of ndhII increases the intracellular NADH/NAD+ ratio in M. tuberculosis.
source: An earlier microbial study by Vilcheze et al. (2005) indicated that the removal of ndhII, a type II NADH dehydrogenase-encoding gene, increases the intracellular NADH/NAD+ ratio, which results in phenotypic resistance to both the front-line anti-TB drug isoniazid (INH) and the related drug ethionamide (ETH).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vilcheze et al., 2005.

claim: Increased intracellular NADH/NAD+ ratio results in phenotypic resistance to isoniazid and ethionamide.
source: An earlier microbial study by Vilcheze et al. (2005) indicated that the removal of ndhII, a type II NADH dehydrogenase-encoding gene, increases the intracellular NADH/NAD+ ratio, which results in phenotypic resistance to both the front-line anti-TB drug isoniazid (INH) and the related drug ethionamide (ETH).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vilcheze et al., 2005.

claim: The de novo and salvage pathways of NAD+ have been proposed as potential targets for anti-TB drugs.
source: Subsequently, the de novo and salvage pathways of NAD+ have been proposed as potential targets for anti-TB drugs (Vilchèze et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vilchèze et al., 2010.

claim: Lysine acetylation is an evolutionarily conserved, reversible post-translational modification in three domains of life.
source: Lysine acetylation is an evolutionarily conserved, reversible post-translational modification in three domains of life (Weinert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weinert et al., 2013.

claim: Pat catalyzes acetylation with acetyl-CoA as the donor of the acetyl group.
source: In general, the acetyl moiety is provided via two distinct mechanisms: i) Pat-catalyzed acetylation (Starai and Escalante-Semerena, 2004) and CobB-aided deacetylation (Starai et al., 2002) with acetyl-CoA as the donor of the acetyl group; and ii) the non-enzymatic action of acetyl-phosphate (AcP) donated by glycolysis (Kakuda et al., 1994; Klein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Starai and Escalante-Semerena, 2004.

claim: CobB catalyzes deacetylation with acetyl-CoA as the donor of the acetyl group.
source: In general, the acetyl moiety is provided via two distinct mechanisms: i) Pat-catalyzed acetylation (Starai and Escalante-Semerena, 2004) and CobB-aided deacetylation (Starai et al., 2002) with acetyl-CoA as the donor of the acetyl group; and ii) the non-enzymatic action of acetyl-phosphate (AcP) donated by glycolysis (Kakuda et al., 1994; Klein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Starai et al., 2002.

claim: Non-enzymatic acetylation can occur via acetyl-phosphate donated by glycolysis.
source: In general, the acetyl moiety is provided via two distinct mechanisms: i) Pat-catalyzed acetylation (Starai and Escalante-Semerena, 2004) and CobB-aided deacetylation (Starai et al., 2002) with acetyl-CoA as the donor of the acetyl group; and ii) the non-enzymatic action of acetyl-phosphate (AcP) donated by glycolysis (Kakuda et al., 1994; Klein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kakuda et al., 1994; Klein et al., 2007.

claim: Lysine acetylation is linked to central metabolism via acetyl-CoA synthetase in Mycobacterium.
source: Not surprisingly, the lysine acetylation is linked to central metabolism via acetyl-CoA synthetase (Xu et al., 2011) and the biosynthesis of siderophore, an intracellular iron chelator (Vergnolle et al., 2016) in Mycobacterium.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2011.

claim: Lysine acetylation is linked to the biosynthesis of siderophore in Mycobacterium.
source: Not surprisingly, the lysine acetylation is linked to central metabolism via acetyl-CoA synthetase (Xu et al., 2011) and the biosynthesis of siderophore, an intracellular iron chelator (Vergnolle et al., 2016) in Mycobacterium.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vergnolle et al., 2016.

claim: A universal stress protein (USP) is acetylated with the cAMP-dependent Pat acetyltransferase (MSMEG_5458) in M. smegmatis.
source: A universal stress protein (USP) is acetylated with the cAMP-dependent Pat acetyltransferase (MSMEG_5458) in M. smegmatis (Nambi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nambi et al., 2010.

claim: The genes nadA, nadB, and nadC are organized as an operon adjacent to nrtR on the chromosome of Mycobacterium species.
source: Genome context analyses suggested that the genes that encode the enzymes involved in the initial three steps of NAD+ synthesis (nadA/nadB/nadC) are organized in a conserved manner as an operon and located adjacent to a Nudix related transcriptional regulator (nrtR) on the chromosome of Mycobacterium species (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by genome context analysis and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A 23-bp NrtR-binding palindrome is conservatively located between the nrtR and nadA/B/C operons in mycobacteria.
source: We identified a 23-bp NrtR-binding palindrome conservatively located between the nrtR and nadA/B/C operons in mycobacteria (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The sequence of the NrtR-binding motif in Mycobacterium species is 5′-GTTTTCGA-N7-TCGAAAAC-3′.
source: The sequence of the NrtR-binding motif in Mycobacterium species [5′-GTTTTCGA-N7-TCGAAAAC-3′] is significantly different from that in Streptococcus [5′-ATA-N-TTTA-N3-TAAAA-N2-ATA-3′] (Wang et al., 2019) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 1C and comparison with Streptococcus.

claim: The NrtR-binding motif in Mycobacterium is significantly different from that in Streptococcus.
source: The sequence of the NrtR-binding motif in Mycobacterium species [5′-GTTTTCGA-N7-TCGAAAAC-3′] is significantly different from that in Streptococcus [5′-ATA-N-TTTA-N3-TAAAA-N2-ATA-3′] (Wang et al., 2019) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 1B and supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: De novo NAD+ synthesis is very conserved in different Mycobacterium species.
source: The most important clue is that de novo NAD+ synthesis is very conserved in different Mycobacterium species, enabling the use of Mycobacterium smegmatis as a model that can be used to study the regulatory mechanism for the de novo NAD+ synthesis pathway.
evidence: This is based on genome context analysis shown in Figure 1A and represents an inference from comparative genomics.

claim: 260 Nudix protein family representatives were selected from diverse bacterial species for phylogenetic analysis.
source: A maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree was constructed using 260 Nudix protein family representatives selected from diverse bacterial species (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A common feature of NrtR homologs is the invariant presence of the N-terminal Nudix domain fused with a characteristic C-terminal domain.
source: A common feature of the NrtR homologs is the invariant presence of the N-terminal Nudix domain (PF00293 or COG1051) fused with a characteristic C-terminal domain (PB002540), which is similar to the C-terminal part of proteins from the uncharacterized COG4111 family (Srouji et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on domain analysis and supported by citation to Srouji et al., 2017.

claim: NrtR evolved through the fusion of an ADPR-preferring Nudix hydrolase to a diversified DNA-binding domain.
source: The data analyzed in this study suggest an evolutionary scenario for NrtR that includes the fusion of an ADPR-preferring Nudix hydrolase to a diversified DNA-binding domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Six residues in the DNA-binding domain of MsNrtR (D167, T169, N170, R173, K179, and R196) are crucial for its DNA-binding ability.
source: In total, six residues in its DNA-binding domain (namely D167, T169, N170, R173, K179, and R196) were predicted to be crucial for its DNA-binding ability (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 3A-B and validated by mutagenesis experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: MsNrtR binds specifically to the nrtR probe.
source: The electrophoresis mobility shift assay (EMSA) confirmed that MsNrtR binds specifically to the nrtR probe (Figure 3C), rather than to an irrelevant DNA probe (such as the promoter of vprA, which encodes a response regulator of V. cholerae, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3C and negative control in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The binding affinity (KD) of MsNrtR to the cognate DNA probe is around 1530 nM.
source: In addition, SPR evaluated the binding affinity of MsNrtR to the cognate DNA probe (i.e., KD, the equilibrium dissociation constant, was around 1530 nM, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on SPR measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Each of the six MsNrtR mutants (D167A, T169A, N170A, R173A, R196A, and K179A) lost their DNA-binding ability.
source: In contrast to the wild-type protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C), each of these MsNrtR mutants (D167A [Figure 3—figure supplement 3D], T169A [Figure 3—figure supplement 3E], N170A [Figure 3—figure supplement 3F], R173A [Figure 3—figure supplement 3G], R196A [Figure 3—figure supplement 3H], and K179A [Figure 3—figure supplement 3I]) consistently lost their DNA-binding ability in our gel shift assays.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-I.

claim: MsNrtR does not have apparent ADPR pyrophosphohydrolase activity in the presence of Mg2+ or Mn2+.
source: Consistent with this alignment, we could not detect any apparent ADPR pyrophosphohydrolase activity in the presence of Mg2+ or Mn2+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is based on enzymatic assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4E.

claim: 50 mM of ADP-ribose can significantly release MsNrtR from DNA.
source: As expected, we observed that 50 mM of ADP-ribose can significantly release MsNrtR from DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on EMSA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The three adjacent genes nadA, nadB and nadC are transcribed in an operon.
source: The results of PCR combined with reverse transcriptional PCR (RT-PCR) proved that the three adjacent genes nadA, nadB and nadC are transcribed in an operon (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The removal of nrtR provides a 2- to 6-fold increase in the expression of the nadA/B/C operon compared with the wild type.
source: Subsequently, real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) demonstrated that the removal of nrtR provides a 2- to 6-fold increase of the expression of the nadA/B/C operon compared with that in the WT (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The levels of intracellular NAD+ and NADH in the ΔnrtR mutant are higher than those in the wild type.
source: In accordance with the qRT-PCR results (Figure 4B), the levels of intracellular NAD+ and NADH in the ΔnrtR mutant are higher than those in the WT, suggesting that NrtR acts as a repressor for homeostasis of the NAD+(NADH) pool (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is based on NAD+ and NADH measurements shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Deletion of nrtR causes a dramatic increase in the LacZ activity of nrtR-lacZ.
source: Consequently, we found that deletion of nrtR causes a dramatic increase in the LacZ activity of nrtR-lacZ on agar plates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on lacZ fusion assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The amplitude for auto-repression of nrtR is constantly around 8- to 10-fold, regardless of the growth stage of the bacteria.
source: Intriguingly, the amplitude for auto-repression of nrtR is constantly around 8- to 10-fold, regardless of the growth stage of the bacteria (ranging from lag phase in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and mid-log phase in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, to equilibrium stage in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on β-galactosidase assays at different growth phases shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: The recombinant MsNrtR is constantly acetylated, regardless of whether E. coli or M. smegmatis was used as the expression host.
source: Unexpectedly, Western blotting elucidated that the recombinant MsNrtR is constantly acetylated, regardless of whether Escherichia coli or M. smegmatis was used as the expression host (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Five acetylated lysine sites were identified in MsNrtR by LC/MS analysis.
source: To further consolidate this observation, the MsNrtR protein was subjected to peptide mass fingerprinting through LC/MS (LTQ Orbitrap Elite) analysis. Of the five acetylated lysine sites that we identified, the Lys134 (K134) acetylation site is highly conserved in NrtR homologs from different species (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on LC/MS analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Lys134 (K134) acetylation site is highly conserved in NrtR homologs from different species.
source: To further consolidate this observation, the MsNrtR protein was subjected to peptide mass fingerprinting through LC/MS (LTQ Orbitrap Elite) analysis. Of the five acetylated lysine sites that we identified, the Lys134 (K134) acetylation site is highly conserved in NrtR homologs from different species (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: K134 is located at the junction between the N-terminal Nudix domain and the C-terminal HTH domain.
source: Structural analysis suggested that K134 is located at the junction between the N-terminal Nudix domain and the C-terminal HTH domain (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The K134A mutant protein cannot be acetylated efficiently.
source: In addition, it seems likely that acetylation of K134 is a prevalent form because the K134A mutant protein cannot be acetylated efficiently (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The DNA-binding abilities of the three MsNrtR mutants (K134R, K134Q and K134A) are impaired to varying degrees compared with the wild-type protein.
source: However, the EMSA experiments verified that the DNA-binding abilities of the aforementioned three protein mutants (K134R [Figure 5—figure supplement 1D], K134Q [Figure 5—figure supplement 1E] and K134A [Figure 5—figure supplement 1F]) are impaired to varying degrees when compared with their parental version (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: This is based on EMSA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-G.

claim: There is no difference in the acetylation levels of the MsNrtR proteins of WT, Δpat and ΔcobB.
source: By contrast, we detected no difference in the acetylation levels of the MsNrtR proteins of WT, Δpat and ΔcobB (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The percentage of acetylated NrtR increased in a time-dependent manner when incubated with AcP.
source: This showed clearly that the percentage of acetylated NrtR increased in a time-dependent manner (Figure 6D and F).
evidence: This is based on in vitro acetylation assays shown in Figure 6D and F.

claim: NrtR acetylation occurred in an AcP-dose-dependent manner.
source: This acetylation also occurred in an AcP-dose-dependent manner (Figure 6E and G).
evidence: This is based on in vitro acetylation assays shown in Figure 6E and G.

claim: The acetylation level of MsNrtR in the double mutant (ΔackA+Δpta) is reduced 4–5-fold when compared with its parental strain.
source: The acetylation level of MsNrtR in the double mutant of M. smegmatis (ΔackA+Δpta), is reduced 4–5-fold when compared with its parental strain (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 6H-I.

claim: The removal of a single ackA only slightly repressed the acetylation of MsNrtR growing under inducing conditions of either 0.2% glucose or 1.0% acetate.
source: In M. smegmatis, the removal of a single ackA only slightly repressed the acetylation of MsNrtR growing under inducing conditions of either 0.2% glucose or 1.0% acetate (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 6H-I.

claim: The K134Q mutation led to a three-fold upregulation in nrtR transcription.
source: In general agreement with the positive control, the K134Q mutation led to a three-fold upregulation in nrtR transcription (Figure 7A), Similar scenarios were also observed for the other two point-mutants, K134A and K134R, despite the lower level of (close to two-fold) of regulatory dysfunction in the control of nrtR transcription (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on lacZ fusion assays shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Functional impairment of the K134 acetylation site can increase the transcriptional level of the nadABC operon 2–3-fold.
source: RT-qPCR assays showed that functional impairment of the K134 acetylation site can increase the transcriptional level of the nadABC operon 2–3-fold (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The pool of intracellular NAD+ in the K134 point-mutants accumulated to a level that was 2–3-fold that in the wild-type strain.
source: More importantly, the pool of intra-cellular NAD+ in the K134 point-mutants accumulated to a level that was 2–3-fold that in the wild-type strain (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on NAD+ measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Inactivation of the AcP pathway led to a significant increase in the β-gal level of nrtR-lacZ transcriptional fusion.
source: As anticipated, inactivation of the AcP pathway (especially in the Δpta+ΔackA double mutan having AcP level of ~10 μM, largely lower than that of the parental strain, ~460 μM) led to a significant increase in the β-gal level of nrtR-lacZ transcriptional fusion (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is based on lacZ fusion assays shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The cytosolic pools of both NAD+ and NADH were increased 2.5–3-fold in the double mutant (Δpta+ΔackA).
source: In particular, the cytosolic pools of both NAD+ (Figure 8C) and NADH (Figure 8D) were increased 2.5–3-fold in the double mutant (Δpta+ΔackA), which is deficient in the AcP pathway.
evidence: This is based on NAD+ and NADH measurements shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: 17% of the enzymes of central metabolism that are essential for the survival of M. tuberculosis require the NAD+ cofactor.
source: It has been estimated that 17% of the enzymes of central metabolism that are essential for the survival of M. tuberculosis require the NAD+ cofactor (Beste et al., 2007), regardless of the organism's state of latency or active-replication (Rodionova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beste et al., 2007.

claim: The NAD+ metabolic pathway and its regulatory mechanism have been recognized as an attractive target for the development of new anti-TB therapeutics.
source: It is rational that the NAD+ metabolic pathway and its regulatory mechanism have been recognized as an attractive target for the development of new anti-TB therapeutics (Rodionova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodionova et al., 2014.

claim: MsNrtR retains only the ability to bind cognate DNA and loses its ADP-ribose hydrolase activity.
source: Although it structurally comprises an N-terminal Nudix domain and a C-terminal Helix-Turn-Helix motif (Huang et al., 2009), MsNrtR retains only the ability to bind cognate DNA (Figure 3) and loses its ADP-ribose hydrolase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on DNA-binding assays (Figure 3) and enzymatic assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E) combined with citation to Huang et al., 2009.

claim: The genome of M. smegmatis contains 29 predicted proteins of the Nudix hydrolase family.
source: This prediction is in part (if not entirely) explained by the genome-wide distribution of 29 predicted proteins of the Nudix hydrolase family in M. smegmatis (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on genome analysis presented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The S. suis NrtR has an inactive Nudix hydrolase domain.
source: A similar scenario in which the S. suis NrtR has an inactive Nudix hydrolase domain (Wang et al., 2019) allowed us to further hypothesize that most members of the Nudix-related regulator family might initially recruit ancient Nudix hydrolase as a signaling module, and then un-necessitate its enzymatic function while retaining its regulatory role as an evolutionary relic (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Most members of the Nudix-related regulator family might initially recruit ancient Nudix hydrolase as a signaling module, and then lose its enzymatic function while retaining its regulatory role.
source: A similar scenario in which the S. suis NrtR has an inactive Nudix hydrolase domain (Wang et al., 2019) allowed us to further hypothesize that most members of the Nudix-related regulator family might initially recruit ancient Nudix hydrolase as a signaling module, and then un-necessitate its enzymatic function while retaining its regulatory role as an evolutionary relic (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from phylogenetic analysis and observations in multiple species, supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: The NrtR of Pseudomonas participates in the fitness and virulence of this pathogen within mice.
source: Because the NrtR of Pseudomonas participates in the fitness and virulence of this pathogen within mice (Okon et al., 2017), it is very interesting to wonder how NrtR and its regulated route of NAD+ synthesis contribute to the survival and chronic infection of Mycobacterium within the host environment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Okon et al., 2017.

claim: Protein acetylation is a ubiquitous form of post-translational modification in prokaryotes.
source: Protein acetylation is a ubiquitous form of post-translational modification in prokaryotes (Ren et al., 2017), which is implicated in central metabolism and even bacterial pathogenicity (Ren et al., 2019; Sang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ren et al., 2017.

claim: Protein acetylation is implicated in central metabolism and bacterial pathogenicity.
source: Protein acetylation is a ubiquitous form of post-translational modification in prokaryotes (Ren et al., 2017), which is implicated in central metabolism and even bacterial pathogenicity (Ren et al., 2019; Sang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ren et al., 2019; Sang et al., 2016.

claim: A global acetylome analysis of M. tuberculosis identified almost 137 unique acetylated proteins involved in diverse biological processes.
source: A global acetylome analysis of M. tuberculosis by Ge and coworkers (Liu et al., 2014) identified almost 137 unique acetylated proteins that are involved in diverse biological processes, some of which had undergone lysine acetylation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: K47 acetylation in M. smegmatis BioQ regulates biotin metabolism.
source: In fact, our research group very recently affirmed the presences of such a modification of K47 in the M. smegmatis BioQ that regulates biotin metabolism (Tang et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2018.

claim: The synthesis and utilization of biotin is necessary for survival and infectivity of intracellular pathogens.
source: In light of the facts that i) mycobacterial NAD+ metabolism is regarded as an promising drug target (Bi et al., 2011; Rodionova et al., 2014) and ii) the synthesis and utilization of biotin is necessary for survival and infectivity of intracellular pathogens (Park et al., 2015; Bockman et al., 2015; Woong Park et al., 2011), we hypothesized that lysine acetylation plays an indispensable role in bacterial virulence.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Park et al., 2015; Bockman et al., 2015; Woong Park et al., 2011.

claim: Lysine acetylation plays an indispensable role in bacterial virulence.
source: In light of the facts that i) mycobacterial NAD+ metabolism is regarded as an promising drug target (Bi et al., 2011; Rodionova et al., 2014) and ii) the synthesis and utilization of biotin is necessary for survival and infectivity of intracellular pathogens (Park et al., 2015; Bockman et al., 2015; Woong Park et al., 2011), we hypothesized that lysine acetylation plays an indispensable role in bacterial virulence.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the roles of NAD+ and biotin metabolism in pathogenesis, supported by multiple citations.

claim: K201 acetylation of PhoP is involved in Salmonella virulence.
source: This is generally consistent with the K201 acetylation of PhoP, a response regulator of the two-component system in Salmonella virulence (Ren et al., 2016; Ren et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ren et al., 2016; Ren et al., 2019.

claim: The lysine acetylation of NrtR represents an evolutionarily conserved mechanism by which pathogens develop successful infections within the host niche.
source: Given that the acetylation of NrtR paralogs is also detected in two additional pathogenic species, the Gram-negative V. cholerae and Gram-positive S. suis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), it is possible that the lysine acetylation of NrtR represents an evolutionarily conserved mechanism by which a group of pathogens develop successful infections within the nutrition-limited tough host niche.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the detection of acetylation in multiple pathogenic species (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: The AcP-dependent acetylation of K134 is necessary for NrtR to regulate the homeostasis of NAD+ in Mycobacterium.
source: Therefore, the data suggest that the AcP-dependent acetylation of K134 is necessary for NrtR to regulate the homeostasis of NAD+ in Mycobacterium.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing that disruption of the AcP pathway or K134 mutations lead to altered NAD+ homeostasis (Figures 7 and 8).

claim: NrtR regulates NAD+ de novo synthesis and coordinates it with the salvage pathway to maintain NAD+ homeostasis.
source: Therefore, we anticipate that NrtR regulates NAD+ de novo synthesis and coordinates it with the salvage pathway to maintain NAD+ homeostasis (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on the genomic context analysis and illustrated in Figure 1E, representing an inference from the data.

claim: The NrtR-recognizable palindrome is located in the intergenic region between nrtR and nadABC.
source: We identified a 23-bp NrtR-binding palindrome conservatively located between the nrtR and nadA/B/C operons in mycobacteria (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and 1C, demonstrating the location of the palindrome in the intergenic region.

claim: The two NrtR homologs in Mycobacterium and Streptococcus are not functionally exchangeable.
source: This may reflect the fact that these two NrtR homologs are not functionally exchangeable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the significant difference in DNA-binding motifs between the two species.

claim: ADP-ribose is a ligand for the MsNrtR regulator.
source: Obviously, ADP-ribose is a ligand for the MsNrtR regulator.
evidence: This is based on the observation that ADP-ribose can disrupt NrtR-DNA binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).

claim: NrtR acts as a repressor for homeostasis of the NAD+(NADH) pool.
source: In accordance with the qRT-PCR results (Figure 4B), the levels of intracellular NAD+ and NADH in the ΔnrtR mutant are higher than those in the WT, suggesting that NrtR acts as a repressor for homeostasis of the NAD+(NADH) pool (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of nrtR increases NAD+ and NADH levels.

claim: The auto-repressor NrtR negatively regulates the expression of nadABC to maintain the homeostasis of the NAD+(NADH) pool in Mycobacterium.
source: Thus, we concluded that the auto-repressor, NrtR, negatively regulates the expression of nadABC to maintain the homeostasis of the NAD+(NADH) pool in Mycobacterium.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including RT-qPCR, NAD+ measurements, and lacZ fusion assays (Figure 4).

claim: Acetylation of K134 might have a physiological role in NAD+ synthesis.
source: This hints at a possibility that an acetylation of K134 might have a physiological role in NAD+ synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that K134 mutations impair DNA-binding ability (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: AcP donates the acetyl group for the post-translational acetylation of NrtR.
source: Obviously, these findings constitute in vitro evidence that AcP donates the acetyl group for the post-translational acetylation of NrtR (Figure 6D–G).
evidence: This is based on in vitro acetylation assays with AcP shown in Figure 6D-G.

claim: The K134 acetylation of MsNrtR is physiologically dependent on the AckA/Pta-containing route for AcP formation.
source: Along with the in vitro data, the in vivo evidence allowed us to conclude that the K134 acetylation of MsNrtR is physiologically dependent on the AckA/Pta-containing route for AcP formation (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on both in vitro and in vivo experimental data (Figure 6).

claim: Natural selection/evolution has rendered the hydrolyzing ADP-ribose NrtR inactive to avoid functional redundancy.
source: It seems likely that natural selection/evolution has rendered the hydrolyzing ADP-ribose NrtR inactive in order to avoid functional redundancy.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that MsNrtR lacks enzymatic activity and the presence of many other Nudix proteins in the genome.

claim: The NrtR orthologs of S. suis and M. smegmatis are antagonized by ADP-ribose in binding to cognate DNA targets.
source: Consistent with earlier descriptions (Rodionov et al., 2008b), the NrtR orthologs of S. suis (Wang et al., 2019) and M. smegmatis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) proved to be antagonized by ADP-ribose in the binding to cognate DNA targets.
evidence: This is based on experimental data (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) and supported by citations to Rodionov et al., 2008b and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: The NrtR (NdnR) of Corynebacterium glutamicum exhibits more affinity to binding the DNA probe in the presence of NAD+.
source: By contrast, the NrtR (also named NdnR) of Corynebacterium glutamicum, a close relative of Mycobacterium, has surprisingly been found to exhibit more affinity to binding the DNA probe in the presence of NAD+ (Teramoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Teramoto et al., 2012.

claim: The varied configuration of signaling module within different NrtR orthologs explains the different responses to NAD+ and ADP-ribose.
source: This is probably explained by the varied configuration of signaling module within different NrtR orthologs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the different ligand responses observed in different NrtR orthologs.
